section.title: The Vision of the Glory of God
section.sectionRationale: The book opens not in Jerusalem but by a canal in Babylon, among a defeated and displaced people. There, of all places, the heavens open and a priest turned exile sees the glory of the LORD, mobile, sovereign, and undiminished, enthroned above a storm of living creatures and whirling wheels.
section.thesis: Even among the exiles by a foreign river, the glory of God appears enthroned and on the move, teaching Israel, and every reader since, that the LORD is not confined to a ruined temple or a lost land but reigns wherever His people are found.
section.frameNote: Five scenes: the priest among the exiles; the storm and the four living creatures; the wheels within wheels; the crystal expanse and the throne above it; and the appearance of the glory of the LORD.

units.label: A priest among the exiles
units.note: the heavens open by the Kebar

verses.text: In the thirtieth year, on the fifth day of the fourth month, while I was among the exiles by the River Kebar, the heavens opened and I saw visions of God.
On the fifth day of the month, it was the fifth year of the exile of King Jehoiachin,
the word of the LORD came directly to Ezekiel the priest, the son of Buzi, in the land of the Chaldeans by the River Kebar. And there the LORD's hand was upon him.

units.label: The storm and the living creatures
units.note: four faces, four wings, one movement

verses.text: I looked and saw a whirlwind coming from the north, a great cloud with fire flashing back and forth and brilliant light all around it. In the center of the fire was a gleam like {{chashmal|amber}},
and within it was the form of four living creatures. And this was their appearance: They had a human form,
but each had four faces and four wings.
Their legs were straight, and the soles of their feet were like the hooves of a calf, gleaming like polished bronze.
Under their wings on their four sides they had human hands. All four living creatures had faces and wings,
and their wings were touching one another. They did not turn as they moved; each one went straight ahead.
The form of their faces was that of a man, and each of the four had the face of a lion on the right side, the face of an ox on the left side, and also the face of an eagle.
Such were their faces. Their wings were spread upward; each had two wings touching the wings of the creature on either side, and two wings covering its body.
Each creature went straight ahead. Wherever the {{ruach|spirit}} would go, they would go, without turning as they moved.

In the midst of the living creatures was the appearance of glowing coals of fire, or of torches. Fire moved back and forth between the living creatures; it was bright, and lightning flashed out of it.
The creatures were darting back and forth as quickly as flashes of lightning.

units.label: Wheels within wheels
units.note: the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels

verses.text: When I looked at the living creatures, I saw a wheel on the ground beside each creature with its four faces.
The workmanship of the wheels looked like the gleam of beryl, and all four had the same likeness. Their workmanship looked like a wheel within a wheel.
As they moved, they went in any of the four directions, without pivoting as they moved.
Their rims were high and awesome, and all four rims were full of eyes all around.
So as the living creatures moved, the wheels moved beside them, and when the creatures rose from the ground, the wheels also rose.
Wherever the spirit would go, they would go, and the wheels would rise alongside them, because the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels.

When the creatures moved, the wheels moved; when the creatures stood still, the wheels stood still; and when the creatures rose from the ground, the wheels rose alongside them, because the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels.

units.label: The expanse and the throne
units.note: a throne above the crystal expanse

verses.text: Spread out above the heads of the living creatures was the likeness of an awesome expanse, gleaming like crystal.
And under the expanse, their wings stretched out toward one another. Each one also had two wings covering its body.
When the creatures moved, I heard the sound of their wings like the roar of many waters, like the voice of the Almighty, like the tumult of an army. When they stood still, they lowered their wings.
And there came a voice from above the expanse over their heads as they stood still with their wings lowered.
Above the expanse over their heads was the likeness of a throne with the appearance of sapphire, and on the throne high above was a figure like that of a man.

units.label: The appearance of the glory of the LORD

verses.text: From what seemed to be His waist up, I saw a gleam like amber, with what looked like fire within it all around. And from what seemed to be His waist down, I saw what looked like fire; and brilliant light surrounded Him.

The appearance of the brilliant light all around Him was like that of a rainbow in a cloud on a rainy day. This was the appearance of the likeness of the {{kavod|glory}} of the LORD. And when I saw it, I fell facedown and heard a voice speaking.

kavod.gloss: Glory, weight, splendor, the visible manifest presence of God. Elsewhere the kavod fills the tabernacle and the temple; here it appears beside a canal in Babylon, teaching the exiles that the LORD's glory is not chained to Jerusalem's ruins but reigns wherever He chooses to reveal Himself.

ruach.gloss: Spirit, wind, breath. The same word describes the stormy wind out of the north and the living spirit that animates the creatures and the wheels, so that the whole moving throne is driven by God's own life-giving Spirit rather than by any mechanism.

chashmal.gloss: A rare and difficult word, traditionally rendered amber or gleaming metal, an alloy of fire and brightness. Its very obscurity fits the scene: Ezekiel reaches for the nearest ordinary words, amber, sapphire, crystal, to gesture at a glory that finally exceeds them all.

basic.context: Ezekiel is a priest, but he is not in the temple. He is a captive among captives, sitting by an irrigation canal in Babylon five years into the exile. There, of all unlikely places, the heavens open and he sees a vision of God: a storm from the north, four strange living creatures, wheels within wheels full of eyes, a crystal expanse, and above it all a throne with a figure like a man, blazing with light like a rainbow in the clouds.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real inaugural vision that commissions Ezekiel as a prophet, told in the layered, groping language apocalyptic visions use when human words strain to describe divine reality. Readers should hold the details, the faces, the wheels, the colors, with humility rather than pressing them into a technical blueprint; the vision's unmistakable center is that the glory of God is present, mobile, and sovereign even in exile.
basic.originalLanguages: The great word is kavod, glory, the weighty, visible presence of God, seen here far from Jerusalem. The wheels and creatures move by the ruach, the spirit or wind of God, and the flashing brightness at the heart of the fire is called chashmal, a rare Hebrew word usually rendered amber, itself a sign of glory too bright for ordinary language.
basic.typology: The mobile throne, resting on no fixed foundation, anticipates a presence of God no longer confined to one building. The four living creatures reappear around God's throne in Revelation 4, now joined by worship of the Lamb, and the man like a figure on the throne anticipates the day when God's glory is seen in a true man, Jesus Christ.
basic.christ: John writes that Isaiah, in his own throne vision, saw Christ's glory and spoke about Him, John 12:41; the same principle stands here. The kavod enthroned above the cherubim in Ezekiel 1 is the same glory the apostle John says was seen in the flesh in Jesus, who 'became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen His glory,' John 1:14. What Ezekiel glimpsed veiled in storm and fire, the church has seen unveiled in the face of Christ.
basic.god: God is transcendent and holy, so overwhelming that the prophet can only describe Him by likeness upon likeness, yet He is also present and near, appearing not in the temple courts but beside a ditch in a pagan empire. His throne is not fixed to one place; wherever His exiled people are, His glory can be found.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 6 pictures a similar throne vision at the prophet's call. Revelation 4 gathers four living creatures and a throne like this one before the Lamb. John 1:14 and 12:41 identify the glory of God, seen by the prophets, with the glory of Jesus Christ.
basic.oneStory: The story of the Bible is the story of God's glory dwelling with His people, lost through sin, exiled with Israel, and finally returned to dwell among us in Jesus Christ, whose glory outshines every vision, and who will one day fill the new creation the way the kavod once filled the tabernacle.

context.literary:
The opening verses are a double introduction. Verses 1 to 3 give the setting twice, once in the first person ('I saw visions of God') and once in the third ('the word of the LORD came directly to Ezekiel the priest'). The slide from 'I' to 'he' is unusual and has puzzled editors, but it fits a book in which the prophet is both a witness and a man spoken about. The Hebrew of verse 3 uses an emphatic form, 'the word came, it came', which the BSB renders 'came directly'. The prophet's name is given only here and in 24:24, and the mention of 'the hand of the LORD' announces a refrain that returns at 3:14, 8:1, 37:1 and 40:1, each time at the head of a major vision.

The vision itself is organised in descending order from the world to the throne. The storm in verse 4, the creatures in verses 5 to 14, the wheels in verses 15 to 21, the expanse in verses 22 to 25 and the throne in verses 26 to 28 move the eye steadily upward, and each layer ends where the next begins. The prose is strained to the breaking point. The words 'like' and 'appearance' and 'likeness' recur until the account is almost all comparison, and verse 28 compresses the problem into a phrase of three removes: 'the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD'. The prophet is telling the reader that he saw the thing as near as words can tell.

The chapter also frames the whole book. The glory seen here by the Kebar is seen again leaving the temple in chapters 9 to 11, and it comes back from the east in chapter 43, when the prophet says the vision is like the one by the Kebar, 43:3. The last line of the book, 48:35, names the city 'THE LORD IS THERE'. Chapter 1 is the first panel of a long movement of departure and return.
context.historical:
The date formula matters. The 'fifth year of the exile of King Jehoiachin' in verse 2 falls around 593 BC, four years after Nebuchadnezzar took the king, the officials, the craftsmen and ten thousand others to Babylon, 2 Kings 24:14-16. Jerusalem still stood, and Zedekiah sat on the throne in his place. Among the exiles two voices were competing. Jeremiah wrote them a letter telling them to build houses, plant gardens and seek the city's welfare, Jeremiah 29:4-7, while others promised a swift return. Ezekiel arrives into that dispute as the prophet whose first vision says that the God of Zion has not been left behind.

The setting is a canal, in the Hebrew nehar, in the Babylonian countryside. The exiles had been resettled in farming communities, living by the waterways where the labour was needed. For a priest, the contrast was cruel. His calling was bound to Jerusalem's temple, to a rota of service and a body of ritual that could be carried out only at one altar. A priest in a foreign land was a man whose life's work had been cut off, and the text invites the reader to feel that.

The 'thirtieth year' of verse 1 is the book's first puzzle, because the prophet never says of what it is the thirtieth. A common view is that it is his age, the year at which a priest would have begun his service, Numbers 4:3. Others link it to a reckoning of years from a known royal or religious landmark. Whichever is right, the point for first readers would be the same: the priest who should have been starting his work in the temple is given a greater sanctuary in a stranger's land.

Babylon itself was a world of enormous temples, processions and divine images. Its gods were carried through the streets on festival days. To a people who had seen their own sanctuary burned and its furnishings carried off, Babylon's religion seemed the victor. Ezekiel's first vision is the reply: the enthroned figure is not an idol carried on men's shoulders, and He moves wherever He wishes.
context.canonical:
The vision is a hinge, with a long chain of texts on both sides. The storm of verse 4 recalls the God of Sinai, who came in cloud and fire, and the cherubim recall the ark, where God promised to meet Moses 'above the mercy seat, between the two cherubim', Exodus 25:22. Psalm 18:10 pictures God riding a cherub on the wings of the wind, and Psalm 99:1 calls Him enthroned above the cherubim. The 'pavement of sapphire' under God's feet in Exodus 24:10 is the material of the throne in Ezekiel 1:26, so the elders' sight at Sinai and the exile's sight at the Kebar are two glimpses of one court.

Isaiah 6:1-3 and Daniel 7:9-10 are the nearest relatives. Isaiah saw the Lord on a throne and heard the cry 'Holy, holy, holy'. Daniel saw a throne with burning wheels and a river of fire flowing from it. Ezekiel's account is longer and stranger and is the fountain of the later Jewish reflection on the chariot. The same pattern shows in 1 Kings 8:10-11, where the glory fills Solomon's temple, and in Ezekiel's own later chapters, where it leaves, 9:3 and 11:22-23, and returns, 43:2-5.

The New Testament uses the vision more than it quotes it. John 12:41 says Isaiah saw Jesus' glory, and the book of Revelation re-draws the scene in chapter 4: a throne, a rainbow like an emerald, a sea of glass like crystal, four living creatures full of eyes, and a ceaseless 'Holy, Holy, Holy'. Revelation 1:13-16 gives the figure the likeness of One like the Son of Man, whose voice is 'like the roar of many waters', as the voice of Ezekiel's glory is, Ezekiel 43:2. The picture that began among exiles by a Babylonian canal ends in the book that names the Lamb at the centre of the throne, Revelation 5:6.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Ezekiel's first task is to answer a question the exiles could not say aloud: has the LORD been defeated along with His city? The vision answers in the only way that could be heard, by showing a throne that is bigger than any building and that has come to them. The prophet wants his readers to know, before a word of judgment is spoken, that the one who will send those words is the one who is truly king. Everything that follows in the book, the warnings against Jerusalem and the promises of restoration, depends on the reader believing that this God is present in Babylon.

He also wants them to be frightened in the right way. The vision does not soothe. The prophet falls on his face, and the creatures flash like lightning. The God who has come to the exiles is not a tame tribal deity who has followed His people into trouble. He is the holy King who is free to leave a temple that has become corrupt, as chapters 8 to 11 will show. The comfort of verse 28 is bound up with its terror.

The writer is also careful about what he does not claim. He says 'likeness' and 'appearance' again and again, and he does not say that he saw God Himself in His essence. The first hearers were meant to receive the vision as a true encounter that nevertheless leaves God larger than the report. This keeps the reading humble and the worship alive.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes something Ezekiel saw, not something believers are told to seek. It does not teach that a vision of God's throne is the normal basis of a prophet's authority, still less that Christians should hunt for the chariot in their own experience. The prophet's authority rests on the word of the LORD that came to him, verse 3, and the vision serves that word. Nothing in the passage commands a technique, a posture or a method of seeing.

It also does not prescribe a theory of angels. The faces, the wings, the eyes on the rims and the wheel within a wheel are given in the language of vision, and later interpreters have woven elaborate systems out of them. The text itself changes some of the details when it retells the scene in chapter 10, which warns against treating every phrase as a blueprint. What carries forward is the doctrine the scene teaches: God is enthroned, mobile, holy and near to His people in a place of exile.

The right response is shown by the prophet. He falls on his face and he listens, verse 28. For believers, that means worship and a readiness to hear, not a hunger for spectacle. It also means that those in hard and unfamiliar places can be sure that God has not stayed behind.

debates.question: What are the four living creatures?

views.label: Cherubim, the same beings named later in the vision
views.case: Ezekiel himself identifies these creatures as cherubim in Ezekiel 10:20, the same order of angelic being that guarded Eden and overshadowed the ark, here attending God's throne in glory.

views.label: A symbol gathering all creation before God
views.case: The four faces, man, lion, ox, and eagle, are often read as representing humanity and the noblest of the wild beasts, cattle, and birds, so that all creation is pictured attending and serving the Creator's throne.

debates.bearing: Either reading agrees that the creatures exist to attend and display God's glory; the details serve worship and wonder, not zoological or angelological precision.

debates.question: What do the wheels signify?

views.label: God's total, unhindered sovereignty and presence
views.case: Wheels within wheels, moving in any direction without turning, full of eyes, dramatize that God's throne can go anywhere, see everything, and answer to no obstacle, even the deserts between Jerusalem and Babylon.

views.label: God's vigilant rule over history and nations
views.case: The eyes covering the rims are sometimes read as picturing the all-seeing oversight by which God governs the rise and fall of empires, Babylon included, so that nothing in world events escapes His notice or control.

debates.bearing: Both readings converge on the same pastoral point for exiles: no power on earth, not Babylon's armies nor its gods, can hem in or outrun the LORD who reigns from this throne.

debates.question: What is the 'thirtieth year' in verse 1?

views.label: Ezekiel's own age
views.case: A priest began his service at thirty, Numbers 4:3. On this reading the vision falls in the year when Ezekiel would have entered the temple, and his calling is turned from an altar in Jerusalem to a throne in Babylon. Ancient interpreters such as Origen took the number this way, and it is still the most widely held view.

views.label: A dating era
views.case: Some take the number as a count of years from a notable event, such as a covenant renewal or a royal reign, that the first readers would have recognised. The advantage is that verse 2 supplies a second date for the same event, and the two would then be reckoned by different systems.

debates.bearing: The text does not say, and the main point survives either way. A man whose training had prepared him for temple service is called, at the very moment he might have begun it, to another sort of ministry among exiles.

debates.question: Who is the 'figure like that of a man' in verses 26 to 28?

views.label: God appearing in human likeness
views.case: The text stresses 'likeness' at every step and ends by calling the sight the glory of the LORD. The figure is God showing Himself in a form the prophet can bear, as God had shown Himself to the elders at Sinai, Exodus 24:10, and in the form of a man to others in the early chapters of the Bible.

views.label: The pre-incarnate Son
views.case: Many Christian readers see in the human form on the throne a pre-figuring of the Word who would become flesh, John 1:14, on the ground that the New Testament says the God no one has seen has been made known by the Son, John 1:18, and that Isaiah's throne vision was of Jesus, John 12:41.

debates.bearing: The first view is the safe floor, and the second is a reading the New Testament invites by its own use of throne visions. Either way the lesson holds that the unseen King is willing to meet people in a form that makes Him known, a pattern that finds its fullness in Christ.

study.originalLanguages:
The vision begins with the heavens 'opened', a plain verb of opening, and the prophet calls what he saw mar'ot Elohim, 'visions of God', in the plural. The word 'saw' and its relatives echo across the chapter, but the important grammar is the long series of comparison words. The phrase 'like the appearance of' (ke-mar'eh) comes again and again, and 'likeness' translates demut, a word that in Genesis 1:26 describes humanity's likeness to God. Ezekiel is careful to say that what he saw resembled a man and was not just a man, and the density of 'like' marks the limit of speech.

The creatures are chayyot, 'living beings', from the root for life. They seem alive in a way the prophet cannot otherwise express, and they are twice called 'the living creature' in the singular, as though the four were one body. Verse 9 says they did not 'turn' as they moved, and the idea of going straight forward is repeated in verses 9, 12 and 17. Nothing in this court needs to change direction, because every direction is open.

The Hebrew for 'amber' is chashmal, a word that occurs only in Ezekiel, here, at 1:27 and at 8:2. The BSB footnote suggests 'glowing metal'. It names the brightness at the heart of the fire, and since no other book uses it, its precise meaning is uncertain. That rarity is part of the effect: the prophet has reached for a word that did not already belong to ordinary things.

The word ruach carries three meanings in this chapter. In verse 4 it is the stormy wind, in verse 12 and again in verse 20 it is the spirit that directs the creatures, and the wheels move because 'the spirit of the living creature was in the wheels'. The same Hebrew word will be breath and Spirit in chapter 37, where the dry bones live. Wind, breath and Spirit are not three words here but three faces of a single one.

In verse 22 the 'expanse' is raqia, the very word God used in Genesis 1:6-8 for the dome between the waters. The throne is set above the creation's own boundary, a quiet claim that the one on it made the world. Verse 24 says the sound of the wings was 'like the voice of the Almighty'. The BSB footnote notes that the Hebrew is Shaddai, the old patriarchal name for God, and the 'roar of many waters' recurs in Ezekiel 43:2 when the glory returns.

The throne is of sapphire, sappir, as the pavement was in Exodus 24:10. Verse 28 gives the rainbow, qeshet, the same word as the 'bow' God set in the cloud after the flood, Genesis 9:13. The vision ends with the word kavod, which comes from a root meaning heavy or weighty: the glory is the weight of God's presence, the thing that makes everything else light by comparison. And the prophet falls on his face, the posture of one who has met more than he can carry.

typology.type: The throne that moves to the exiles, 1:1-4, 26
typology.fulfillment: The glory that filled the tabernacle and the temple, Exodus 40:34-35 and 1 Kings 8:10-11, now appears over a canal in a foreign land. The correspondence is between God's dwelling and His people's location. In Christ it deepens: the Word 'became flesh and dwelt among us', John 1:14, using a verb that echoes the tent of meeting, and He says that where two or three gather in His name, He is there, Matthew 18:20. He speaks of the temple of His body, John 2:19-21, and the church becomes a dwelling place for God, Ephesians 2:21-22. The pattern is completed when John sees no temple in the city, because God and the Lamb are its temple, Revelation 21:22. The type falls short in that Ezekiel's glory would still depart and come again, while the presence in Christ is permanent.

typology.type: The figure with the appearance of a man, 1:26-28
typology.fulfillment: The One enthroned in human likeness anticipates the One who is both God and man. Paul calls the Son 'the image of the invisible God', Colossians 1:15, and Hebrews says He is 'the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature', Hebrews 1:3. John's vision of the risen Christ borrows from Ezekiel's glory, with a voice 'like the roar of many waters' and a form blazing like fire, Revelation 1:13-16. The escalation is that Ezekiel saw a likeness, while the apostles saw and touched the Man, 1 John 1:1. The type falls short because the figure in Ezekiel's vision does not die, rise or bear sin, which is what the incarnate Son came to do.

The bow in the cloud was God's sign after the flood that He would not destroy the earth again, Genesis 9:13-16. To see it ringing the throne in a vision of coming judgment is to learn that the covenant of mercy surrounds the One who judges. In Revelation 4:3 a rainbow encircles the throne, and the throne is then approached by the Lamb who was slain, Revelation 5:6. The escalation is that the sign of a promise becomes the person who keeps it. The type is incomplete in that the rainbow promised only that the world would not be flooded, while the cross opens a way to forgiveness and eternal life.

typology.type: The cherubim and the way to God, 1:5-14, 10:20
typology.fulfillment: Ezekiel names the living beings cherubim, the order that guarded Eden, Genesis 3:24, and shadowed the mercy seat, Exodus 25:22. They stand at the edge of God's presence as both guard and attendant. In Christ the barrier is crossed, and the veil with its woven cherubim is torn, Matthew 27:51, so that believers approach with confidence, Hebrews 10:19-20. The same creatures in Revelation 5 do not bar the way but fall down to worship the Lamb together with the elders, Revelation 5:8. The type falls short in that the cherubim remain servants, while the Son sits on the throne itself.

study.christ:
The vision leads to Christ first because the New Testament says that glory has a face. John writes that 'the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen His glory', John 1:14, and Paul says God has made His light shine in our hearts 'to give us the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ', 2 Corinthians 4:6. Ezekiel could only say that he saw 'the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD'. The apostles say that this glory was heard, seen and handled, 1 John 1:1. The prophet fell on his face before a brightness; the church has been shown the face behind the brightness.

It leads to Christ in the figure on the throne. Verse 26 puts a form like a man above the creatures. Daniel 7:13 sees one like a son of man come to the Ancient of Days and receive an everlasting dominion, and Jesus took that title and used it of Himself before the high priest, Mark 14:62. The same blaze of fire and amber is on the lips of John when he writes of the risen Christ in Revelation 1:13-16, and the voice that was like many waters in Ezekiel 43:2 is now His. The throne once thought to carry only the Father has the Lamb at its centre, Revelation 5:6, and the song is addressed to Him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb together, Revelation 5:13.

It leads to Christ by way of the mobility of the glory. A God who can leave a temple and come to a canal is a God whose presence is not bound to a place, and Jesus says so to the woman at the well: worship will be neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem but in spirit and truth, John 4:21-24. When He promises 'I am with you always, even to the end of the age', Matthew 28:20, He is claiming the very presence that Ezekiel saw arrive among the exiles. He also calls His own body the temple that will be raised, John 2:19-21.

It leads to Christ by way of the one who falls down. Ezekiel falls on his face and then hears a voice. John falls at the feet of the risen Lord as though dead and is told, 'Do not be afraid', Revelation 1:17. The terrifying brightness has a hand that touches the fallen.

The reading has limits. The wheels, the eyes and the faces are not coded names for the persons of Jesus' ministry, and the old suggestion that the four faces stand for the four Gospels is a later devotional pattern, not something the text or the apostles say. The links that hold are the ones the New Testament makes itself, the glory, the human form on the throne and the presence among exiles. These show that Ezekiel saw the same Lord whom the Gospels present.
study.god:
The chapter says a great deal about who God is by showing how He is attended. Everything around the throne is in motion and obedient: the creatures move 'wherever the spirit would go', the wheels follow, the lightning darts at His word. Yet the one at the centre does not move at all. He is seated. The stillness of the throne in the middle of the storm is the vision's chief teaching about God, who rules without strain and needs no effort to hold the world together.

He is transcendent and He is near, and the chapter will not let either truth swallow the other. The throne stands above an expanse, a boundary the prophet cannot cross, and the sound of the wings is the voice of the Almighty. Yet the whole apparatus has come to a canal in Babylon, to a captive priest. The doctrine is not that God is partly far and partly near but that the same God who is high above creation chooses to come to the lowest place. Isaiah 66:1 says heaven is His throne and earth His footstool, and Acts 7:48-49 uses the verse to say that He does not dwell in houses made by hand.

He is all-seeing and all-knowing, as the eyes on the rims suggest, and He is free. The throne can go in any of four directions without turning, so no direction is closed to Him. For a people who feared that Babylon's gods had triumphed, this was a statement about the limits of every other power. Isaiah 40:26 says that He calls out the stars by name, and Ezekiel's creatures are a smaller picture of the same order.

He is holy. The brightness, the fire and the rainbow in the cloud are reminders that His presence is not safe in the way a pet is safe. The prophet falls on his face. Later in the book we learn why the glory left the temple, because it had been defiled, and why it will return, so the vision already shows a God whose nearness is a matter of His holiness and mercy and never of human right.

He keeps covenant. The bow in the cloud is the sign God gave after the flood, Genesis 9:13-16, and the sight of it around the throne is a hint that the one who comes to judge is the one who bound Himself to mercy. In worship this means we can stand in awe and still come close. The prayer that fits the vision is the cry of the creatures in Isaiah 6, 'Holy, holy, holy', along with the quiet confidence that the King on the throne is with His people in whatever strange country they find themselves.

crossReferences.note: Isaiah sees the Lord high and exalted with seraphim crying 'Holy'. Ezekiel's scene shares the throne, the winged attendants, the sound of worship and the prophet's collapse, though Ezekiel's emphasis falls on movement and distance rather than the temple.

The elders on Sinai saw the God of Israel with something like a pavement of sapphire beneath His feet. The sapphire throne of Ezekiel 1:26 uses the same stone, which links the vision to the moment the covenant was ratified.

God promises to meet Moses above the mercy seat between two cherubim. Ezekiel's living creatures are later named cherubim, so the exile sees the moving counterpart of the ark's guardians, and the God who spoke above the ark speaks above the creatures.

The cloud and the glory fill Solomon's temple so that the priests cannot stand. Ezekiel is a priest who has lost that house and receives the same glory in a foreign land, which tells him that the presence was never confined to the building.

The prophet says he recognised the creatures as cherubim when he saw them again in the temple vision. The identification resolves the strangeness of chapter 1 and ties the Kebar scene to the guardians of the sanctuary.

The glory rises from the city and stands over the mountain to the east. The vision at the Kebar is the first act of a departure that leaves the temple empty, which is why the exiles' hope in a swift return was a misreading of what God was doing.

The glory returns from the east and enters the temple, and the prophet says the sight is like the one at the Kebar. The first vision is the promise of this one, since the God who came to the exiles will bring them home.

Another exile sees thrones, a river of fire and a throne with flaming wheels. The wheels and fire of Daniel's court show that Ezekiel's imagery shaped the exilic hope of a coming judgment in which the Son of Man receives the kingdom.

John's four living creatures, covered with eyes and crying 'Holy, Holy, Holy', and his throne ringed by a sea like crystal, re-draw Ezekiel's scene. What the prophet saw as a distant storm becomes the centre of worship in heaven.

The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and the apostles saw His glory. The verb for dwelling recalls the tabernacle where God's glory settled, and so the presence that came to exiles by a canal is made permanently present in a person.

John says Isaiah saw Jesus' glory when he saw the throne. By the same principle the glory in Ezekiel's vision is read as the glory that was later revealed in Christ, which is how the New Testament reads all the throne visions.

In the new Jerusalem there is no temple, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple. The long movement that began with a glory leaving a building and finding exiles ends with a city that needs no building, because God Himself is there.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story begins with God placing a man and a woman in a garden where He walked with them, Genesis 3:8. Sin drove them from the place of His presence, and the rest of the story is the long record of God making a way to dwell among His people again. He gives a tabernacle at Sinai and fills it with glory, Exodus 40:34-35. He fills Solomon's temple in the same way, 1 Kings 8:10-11. Then the people profane the place, and the glory departs. Ezekiel 1 stands at the beginning of that departure, and its great surprise is that the glory does not leave the people but goes with them.

For the exiles it was a shock. They had been taught to think of God's presence as attached to Zion, and Zion was the thing they had lost. The vision shows that the throne of the one who made heaven and earth has wheels. God had come to the place of the curse and the captivity, as He had come to Abraham in Mesopotamia, Acts 7:2, long before the temple existed. The promise that God would be 'a sanctuary for a little while' to the scattered, Ezekiel 11:16, grows from this root.

The vision also sets up what comes next in the book and in the Bible. Chapters 8 to 11 explain why the glory had to leave and chapters 36 to 37 promise a new heart and a new Spirit. Chapter 43 sees the glory return, and the last line gives the city the name 'THE LORD IS THERE'. The New Testament shows how that return happens: in Jesus, who is the dwelling of God among people, John 1:14, who tells His hearers that His body is the temple, John 2:19-21, and who sends the Spirit to make His people a temple, 1 Corinthians 3:16 and Ephesians 2:21-22.

The story ends in a city where the throne is again in the middle of God's people. Revelation 4 and 5 show the scene of Ezekiel's vision opened up to include the Lamb, and Revelation 21:3 hears the announcement that God's dwelling is with humanity. The prophet who fell on his face beside a canal receives his answer at the end of the book: the glory that came to the exiles has come to stay, and the whole creation becomes the place where it rests.

sermon.title: The God Who Speaks
sermon.why: Begg preaches directly from Ezekiel 1:1-28, drawing out how the overwhelming, mobile vision of God's glory meets a prophet in exile and still speaks to a God who is never confined by our circumstances.

quiz.q: Where was Ezekiel when he saw this vision of God's glory?

options.text: In the Jerusalem temple during a festival.
options.note: He is a priest, but he is far from the temple, in exile.

options.text: Among the exiles by the River Kebar in Babylon.
options.note: Ezekiel 1:1-3 sets the vision in exile, not in Jerusalem.

options.text: Traveling toward Egypt with refugees.
options.note: The text places him in Babylon, not Egypt.

options.text: Nowhere in particular; the setting is not given.
options.note: The setting by the River Kebar is stated clearly.

quiz.q: What moved the living creatures and the wheels together?

options.text: The wind blowing them along the ground.
options.note: The storm wind opens the vision, but the spirit within governs the movement.

options.text: Nothing; they stood still throughout.
options.note: The creatures and wheels move together repeatedly in the vision.

options.text: The spirit, or ruach, of the living creatures was in the wheels.
options.note: Ezekiel 1:20-21 says the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels.

options.text: A system of gears and axles.
options.note: The vision describes spirit-driven movement, not mechanical parts.

quiz.q: What did Ezekiel see above the crystal expanse over the creatures' heads?

options.text: The ark of the covenant.
options.note: The vision describes a throne in the heavens, not the ark.

options.text: A second set of living creatures.
options.note: It is a throne with a figure upon it, not more creatures.

options.text: An empty expanse with no throne.
options.note: The throne and its occupant are explicitly seen.

options.text: The likeness of a throne, with a figure like a man seated above it.
options.note: Ezekiel 1:26 describes the throne and the human-like figure upon it.

quiz.q: How did Ezekiel respond when he saw the appearance of the glory of the LORD?

options.text: He fell facedown and heard a voice speaking.
options.note: Ezekiel 1:28 records this response of awe and submission.

options.text: He ran away from the river.
options.note: The text describes him falling facedown, not fleeing.

options.text: He argued with the vision.
options.note: His response was worshipful awe, not argument.

options.text: He felt nothing unusual.
options.note: The vision overwhelms him; his response is dramatic, not indifferent.

quiz.q: What does this vision teach the exiles about God's presence?

options.text: God's presence had been left behind in Jerusalem.
options.note: The opposite is true; the glory appears in Babylon itself.

options.text: The exiles were beyond God's reach.
options.note: The vision insists God reaches and reigns even in exile.

options.text: God's glory is mobile and sovereign, not confined to the ruined temple in Jerusalem.
options.note: The whole vision, especially the wheels, portrays a throne that travels and reigns anywhere.

options.text: God only speaks through dreams, never in visible glory.
options.note: This is an actual seen vision of glory, not merely a dream.

questions: Ezekiel saw the glory of God not in the temple but beside a canal among defeated exiles. Where in your own life do you assume God is absent simply because your circumstances look like defeat?

The throne in this vision moves freely in every direction. What would change in your prayers this week if you truly believed God's presence and rule are not confined to your best or most comfortable seasons?

Ezekiel reaches for word after word, 'like,' 'as it were,' to describe what he saw. How does approaching God with humility and wonder, rather than certainty about every detail, shape the way you read Scripture's harder visions?
The wheels were full of eyes, suggesting nothing escapes God's notice. Is there an area of your life or your world's events that you struggle to believe is under God's watchful, sovereign care?
John says the prophets who saw God's glory were in some sense seeing Christ. How does knowing that Jesus is the fullest revelation of the very glory Ezekiel saw change the way you look at Him?

translationNotes.note: The word rendered amber, chashmal, is rare and its precise meaning is uncertain; ancient and modern translators alike have rendered it amber, electrum, or simply gleaming metal.

Spirit here may equally be rendered wind; the same Hebrew word, ruach, carries both senses, and the ambiguity is likely intentional, joining the storm wind to the animating spirit within the creatures.
Sapphire may refer to the gemstone we know or, as some scholars suggest, to lapis lazuli, a deep blue stone well known in the ancient Near East.
